prompt: In an obligation to deliver a specific or determinate thing subject to a suspensive condition, and the object deteriorated without the fault of the debtor, then:

choices.text: The creditor can choose to exact fulfillment and demand damages
The creditor can ask for rescission and demand damages

rationale: Under Art. 1189 of the Civil Code, if a specific thing is lost or deteriorates pending a suspensive condition without the debtor's fault, the impairment is borne by the creditor (res perit creditori), since the debtor is not liable for fortuitous loss/deterioration.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: In conditional obligations to deliver a determinate thing, loss/deterioration without the debtor's fault before the condition is fulfilled is borne by the creditor.

prompt: Which kind of check is considered legal tender?
rationale: Checks, regardless of type (cashier's, manager's, or certified), are not legal tender in the Philippines; only Philippine currency (coins and notes) issued by the BSP is legal tender. Checks are merely conditional payment absent novation or actual encashment.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: No check is legal tender under Philippine law; checks are only a conditional means of payment of an obligation.

prompt: Vivi is indebted to Igaram for P10,000 evidenced by a promissory note. This promissory note was then transferred to Cobra, then Cobra to Vivi. Which mode extinguished the obligation?
rationale: When the note (evidence of the credit) is eventually transferred back to Vivi, the debtor, the characters of creditor and debtor merge in one person, extinguishing the obligation by confusion/merger under Arts. 1275-1277 of the Civil Code.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Confusion or merger extinguishes an obligation when the characters of creditor and debtor are merged in the same person.

prompt: Delay on the part of the creditor
rationale: Mora accipiendi is the delay of the creditor/obligee in accepting the performance of the obligation, as distinguished from mora solvendi (debtor's delay in performing a real or personal obligation).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Mora accipiendi refers to the creditor's unjustified delay in accepting the debtor's tendered performance.

prompt: If a third party pays an obligation with the consent of the debtor, the following are the effects, except:

choices.text: The third party may compel the creditor to accept payment
The third party will be subrogated to the rights of the creditor
The third party is entitled to beneficial reimbursement
None of the choices is an exception

rationale: Under Art. 1236, when a third person pays with the debtor's express or tacit consent, the payor is entitled to reimbursement for the FULL amount paid AND to legal subrogation (Art. 1237), not merely 'beneficial reimbursement' (which applies only where payment is made WITHOUT the debtor's knowledge/against his will, limited to the extent the payment benefited the debtor).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Payment by a third party with the debtor's consent entitles the payor to full reimbursement and legal subrogation to the creditor's rights, unlike payment without consent which only gives beneficial reimbursement.

prompt: D promised to deliver to C the following specific objects and their equivalent values, in the alternative: (1) Cow – P50,000; (2) Horse – P80,000; or (3) Carabao – P70,000. All the things were lost in the order they were mentioned with the fault of the debtor. How much can the creditor collect from the debtor?
rationale: In alternative obligations where the right of choice belongs to the debtor and all the objects are lost through the debtor's fault, the debtor must pay the value of the LAST thing which became impossible (Art. 1204), which here is the Carabao at P70,000.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: In alternative obligations with the debtor holding the right of choice, if all objects are lost through the debtor's fault, the price of the last object lost is what is payable as damages.

prompt: One party cannot revoke or renounce a contract without the consent of the other, nor have it said aside on the ground that he had made a bad bargain. This relates to which fundamental characteristic of a contract?
rationale: The principle of mutuality of contracts (Art. 1308) provides that a contract must bind both parties and its validity/compliance cannot be left to the will of only one of them; a party cannot unilaterally revoke or set aside a contract merely because it turned out to be a bad bargain.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Mutuality of contracts means a contract binds both parties and cannot be revoked or modified at the sole will of one party.

prompt: A contract of lease of real property for a period longer than 1 year must be in writing in order to:
rationale: Under the Statute of Frauds (Art. 1403[2][e]), a lease of real property for more than one year must be in writing (or at least a note/memorandum) to be enforceable by action; it remains valid between the parties even if oral, but cannot be enforced in court absent ratification or partial performance.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Contracts covered by the Statute of Frauds, such as a lease of real property for more than one year, need to be in writing only for enforceability, not validity.

prompt: Statement I: Contracts without cause, or with unlawful cause, produce no effect whatever. Statement II: The cause is unlawful if it is contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order or public policy. Statement III: The statement of a false cause in contracts shall render them void, if it should not be proved that they were founded upon another cause which is true and lawful.

choices.text: All of the statements are incorrect

rationale: All three statements correctly restate the Civil Code provisions on cause: Art. 1352 (contracts without cause or with unlawful cause produce no effect), Art. 1352 (definition of unlawful cause), and Art. 1353 (false cause renders the contract void unless it is proven to be founded upon another true and lawful cause).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A contract is void if it lacks cause, has an unlawful cause, or states a false cause not shown to be founded upon another true and lawful cause.

prompt: In a contract of mutuum or simple loan, the essential elements would be:

choices.text: Consent, object, cause, form and delivery

rationale: Mutuum is a real contract, meaning that in addition to the ordinary essential requisites of contracts (consent, object, cause), delivery of the thing loaned is required for the contract to be perfected; form is not an essential element of mutuum.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Being a real contract, a contract of simple loan (mutuum) requires delivery of the object, in addition to consent, object, and cause, for its perfection.

prompt: A contract entered into between a deaf-mute and a minor is:
rationale: A minor lacks full civil capacity to give consent, making the contract voidable (Art. 1390) at the option of the incapacitated party; a deaf-mute who does not know how to write is likewise considered to have vitiated/incapacitated consent, but the contract is merely voidable, not void, unenforceable, or rescissible.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A contract entered into by a party who lacks full capacity to give consent, such as a minor, is voidable and may be annulled at that party's instance.

prompt: The remedy of the creditor in contracts entered into by his debtor to defraud him:
rationale: Accion pauliana is the rescissory action available to a creditor under Arts. 1177 and 1381(3) to rescind contracts entered into by the debtor in fraud of creditors, when the creditor cannot otherwise recover what is due him.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Accion pauliana is the creditor's remedy to rescind fraudulent alienations made by the debtor that prejudice the creditor's ability to collect.

prompt: What rate applies to overtime that was rendered by the employee during a regular holiday?
rationale: Under the Labor Code, work on a regular holiday is paid 200% of the basic wage; overtime work performed on that same regular holiday is paid an additional 30% of the holiday rate (200% x 130% = 260%).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Overtime work performed on a regular holiday is paid at 260% of the basic daily wage (200% holiday rate plus 30% overtime premium on that rate).

prompt: A victim of VAWC who is employed shall be entitled to a paid leave of upto __ days in addition to other paid leaves:
rationale: Under RA 9262 (Anti-VAWC Law), a woman employee who is a victim of violence is entitled to a paid leave of up to 10 days, extendible when the necessity arises as specified in the protection order, in addition to other paid leaves under existing labor laws.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: RA 9262 grants a victim of violence against women and children who is employed a paid leave of up to 10 days, apart from other statutory leave benefits.

prompt: To be entitled to the monthly pension, a retired member should have contributed at least __ monthly contributions:
rationale: Under the Social Security Law, a member is entitled to a monthly retirement pension only if he/she has paid at least 120 monthly contributions prior to the semester of retirement; otherwise, only a lump-sum benefit is given.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A monthly SSS retirement pension requires at least 120 monthly contributions prior to the semester of retirement; below that threshold, only a lump-sum amount is paid.

prompt: Charlotte Linlin, single, had a miscarriage and wanted to avail of the optional days without pay. How long is her maternity leave?
rationale: Under the Expanded Maternity Leave Law (RA 11210), all female workers, regardless of civil status, are entitled to 105 days of paid maternity leave regardless of the type of delivery (including miscarriage/emergency termination which used to give only 60 days under the old law), plus an option for additional 30 days without pay; the question refers to the 105-day base entitlement.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: RA 11210 grants 105 days of paid maternity leave to all covered female workers regardless of civil status or mode of delivery, with an additional optional 30 days without pay.

prompt: Insurable interest is required to exist only when the insurance takes effect and need not exist when the loss occurs:
rationale: Under the Insurance Code, for life insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time the policy takes effect, but need not exist at the time of loss (death); for property insurance, insurable interest must exist both at the inception of the policy and at the time of loss.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: In life insurance, insurable interest is required only at the time the policy is taken out, unlike property insurance where it must also exist at the time of loss.

prompt: The mortgagor's insurable interest in property given as security is:

choices.text: Upto the value of the property
Upto the original amount of the obligation

rationale: A mortgagor, as owner of the property, retains insurable interest up to the full value of the property (not merely the unpaid balance), since he stands to lose the entire value of the property in case of loss, over and above the mortgage debt.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The mortgagor, being the owner, has insurable interest to the full value of the mortgaged property, while the mortgagee's insurable interest is limited to the unpaid debt.

prompt: The maximum insured amount is limited only upto 500x of the Statutory Minimum Wage in Metro Manila.
rationale: Under the Insurance Code and IC regulations, industrial life insurance (policies with premiums collected periodically, typically weekly/monthly, in small amounts) is capped at a maximum face amount tied to a multiple of the prevailing statutory minimum daily wage rate in Metro Manila.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Industrial life insurance policies are subject to a statutory cap on the maximum insurable amount pegged to a multiple of the Metro Manila minimum wage.

prompt: Which of the following is a property right of a partner that can be the subject of assignment?

choices.text: Right to participate in the management

rationale: Under the Civil Code, the property rights of a partner are: (1) rights in specific partnership property, (2) interest in the partnership, and (3) right to participate in management. Of these, only the partner's INTEREST in the partnership (share of profits/surplus) may validly be assigned; rights to specific partnership property and to management are not assignable since they involve the personal/fiduciary relationship among partners.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Among a partner's property rights, only the partner's interest (share in profits and surplus) is assignable; rights to specific partnership property and management participation are not.

prompt: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the effects of dissolution in a partnership?

choices.text: If the cause of dissolution is Acts, Insolvency or Death, notice will not be necessary to extinguish mutual agency
Contracts with creditors who had no notice of the dissolution would still be binding
The partners are allowed to continue the business after dissolution of the old partnership
None of the choices is incorrect

rationale: Choice (a) is the false/incorrect statement: under Art. 1834, when dissolution is caused by an act of any partner (with the partnership continuing to appear ongoing to third persons), notice IS generally required to extinguish the authority/apparent mutual agency of a partner as to persons who had extended credit prior to dissolution, unless dissolution is by operation of law (e.g., death, insolvency) or the third person had no prior dealings and no knowledge of the partnership.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The extinguishment of a partner's authority to bind the firm after dissolution generally requires notice to third persons who previously dealt with the partnership, except where dissolution results automatically by operation of law.

prompt: King, Queen and Jack formed the Beast Pirates Partnership, Ltd., where Jack is a limited partner. King was in charge of preparing the Certificate of Limited Partnership and failed to submit the same to the SEC. After three years of operations, the partnership had total assets of P12,000,000, while it owed third party creditors P18,000,000. How much will be the liability of the partners?

choices.text: King and Queen for P3M each
King, Queen and Jack for P2M each
No partner is liable to third party creditors

rationale: Failure to file the Certificate of Limited Partnership with the SEC means the limited partnership was never validly formed as such; consequently it is treated as a general partnership, making ALL partners (King, Queen, and Jack, including the supposed limited partner) general partners who are solidarily/pro-rata liable with their separate property for the P6,000,000 deficiency (P18M debts less P12M assets), i.e., P2,000,000 each.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Failure to record the certificate of limited partnership with the SEC results in a de facto general partnership where all partners, including the intended limited partner, are treated as general partners liable to creditors.

prompt: A limited partner shall be treated as a debtor of the partnership in case: I. The contributions are less than that stated in the Certificate of Limited Partnership; II. He does not contribute the additional contributions indicated in the Certificate of Limited Partnership
rationale: Under Art. 1858 of the Civil Code, a limited partner is liable to the partnership as a debtor: (1) for the difference between his actual contribution and the amount stated in the certificate as having been contributed, and (2) for any unpaid additional contribution he agreed to make in the future as stated in the certificate.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A limited partner becomes a debtor of the partnership for any shortfall in stated contributions and for unpaid additional contributions promised in the certificate.

prompt: In a Universal Partnership of All Present Property, profits derived from properties other than those that are contributed are considered

choices.text: Property of the partner only if there is a stipulation to that effect
Property of the partnership only if there is a stipulation to that effect
Property of the partner and any stipulation to the contrary is void
Property of the partnership whether or not there is stipulation

rationale: Under Art. 1778, in a universal partnership of all present property, all property owned by the partners at the time of the constitution becomes common property, but profits from OTHER property acquired subsequently (not contributed) belong to the partnership ONLY if there is an express stipulation to that effect; without such stipulation, the profits remain the partner's own.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: In a universal partnership of all present property, profits from property not contributed become partnership property only upon an express stipulation.

prompt: A partner's right to reimbursement for amounts he may have disbursed in behalf of the partnership is accompanied by an interest from:

choices.text: The time the expense was made
The time the other partners acknowledge the liability

rationale: Under Art. 1796, the partnership must reimburse a partner for amounts he disbursed for the partnership together with interest computed from the time the expense was actually made, not merely from demand or acknowledgment.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A partner is entitled to reimbursement with interest running from the time he actually made the disbursement on behalf of the partnership.

prompt: Under the Revised Corporation Code, if the number of directors of a corporation vested with public interest is 12, how many independent directors are required?
rationale: Under Sec. 22 of the RCC, corporations vested with public interest must have independent directors constituting at least 20% of the board, but in no case less than two (2); 20% of 12 directors = 2.4, which is rounded UP to the next whole number, i.e., 3 independent directors.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Corporations vested with public interest must have independent directors comprising at least 20% of the board (rounded up), but never fewer than two.

prompt: A corporation's stockholders are not liable beyond their capital contribution

choices.text: Piercing the Veil of Corporate Entity

rationale: The doctrine of limited liability limits a stockholder's liability for corporate debts and obligations to the extent of his subscription/capital contribution, in view of the corporation's separate juridical personality.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The doctrine of limited liability confines a stockholder's exposure for corporate obligations to the amount of his capital contribution.

prompt: There is dissolution but no liquidation in: I. Merger; II. Consolidation
rationale: In both merger and consolidation, the constituent corporations are dissolved, but there is no liquidation of assets because all assets, liabilities, and the business of the constituent corporations are automatically absorbed by the surviving (merger) or the new consolidated (consolidation) corporation.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Merger and consolidation both result in dissolution of the constituent corporations without liquidation, since assets and liabilities are automatically transferred to the surviving or new corporation.

prompt: Voluntary dissolution where no creditors are affected would necessitate submission of a request for dissolution with the SEC. A withdrawal of that request can be made in writing signed by the same number of directors, trustees, shareholders, members necessary to request for dissolution. Within how many days can the withdrawal be filed from the time the request for dissolution is filed with the SEC?
rationale: Under the SEC rules implementing Sec. 134 of the RCC on voluntary dissolution where no creditors are affected, a request for withdrawal of the dissolution filing, signed by the same number/percentage required for the dissolution request, may be filed with the SEC within 15 days from the filing of the request for dissolution.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A request for voluntary dissolution not affecting creditors may be withdrawn within 15 days from its filing with the SEC, upon the same consent required to file it.

prompt: Kanjuro is the secretary of Oden, a director in, and the President of, Wano Corporation. In the course of his employment, Kanjuro obtained material non-public information which he shared with his friend Orochi. All three of them purchased shares of Wano Corporation prior to the information becoming public but for Kanjuro he did so after he resigned therefrom. Who may be considered insiders?
rationale: Under the Securities Regulation Code, an 'insider' includes an officer/director of the issuer, a person who obtained material non-public information by reason of a special relationship to the issuer (even a former officer/employee acting on information obtained during employment), and a 'tippee' who knowingly received such information from an insider. Oden (director/President) is clearly an insider; Kanjuro remains an insider even after resignation because he acted on information obtained during his employment; and Orochi, as a tippee who traded knowing the information was material non-public information, is also treated as an insider.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Insider trading liability under the SRC extends to officers/directors, persons who obtained material non-public information by virtue of a relationship with the issuer (even after they leave), and knowing tippees who trade on that information.

prompt: A common share's voting rights can only be limited by the existence of what type of shares?
rationale: Under the RCC, only preferred shares may be deprived of voting rights (except on matters where the law requires a vote of all shareholders regardless of class); common shares generally always carry full voting rights and are only 'limited' in the relative sense that preferred shares may be granted preferences that common shares do not have, but the classic exam concept tested is that non-voting shares must be preferred shares.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Only preferred shares (never common shares) may be deprived of voting rights under the Revised Corporation Code, except on fundamental matters requiring a class vote.

prompt: A member of the board of directors had a transaction with the Corporation where his presence was necessary to constitute a quorum and/or his vote was necessary to approve the transaction. What would be the required votes to ratify this transaction?

choices.text: Majority of the BOD and majority of the stockholders
Majority of the BOD and 2/3 of the stockholders

rationale: Under Sec. 31 of the RCC, a self-dealing director's contract that would otherwise be voidable (because his presence/vote was necessary for board approval) may be ratified by the vote of stockholders representing at least two-thirds (2/3) of the outstanding capital stock, provided full disclosure is made and the contract is fair and reasonable.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A contract of a self-dealing director whose presence or vote was necessary for board approval requires ratification by 2/3 of the outstanding capital stock, with full disclosure and fairness of the contract.

prompt: The number of directors in a non-stock corporation

choices.text: Not less than 5 but not more than 15
May be less than 5 but not more than 15
May be less than 5 and more than 15
Not less than 5 but may be more than 15

rationale: Under Sec. 13 of the RCC, while stock corporations generally must have not fewer than five and not more than fifteen directors, a non-stock corporation's trustees may be more than 15 (subject to what its articles/by-laws provide) and there is no fixed statutory minimum of five, so the number may be less than 5 or more than 15.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Unlike a stock corporation's directors (5 to 15), a non-stock corporation's trustees are not statutorily confined to the 5-to-15 range.

prompt: If a corporation has 10 directors, 8 of which are present in the meeting to elect corporate officers, how many votes are required?
rationale: Election of corporate officers requires the vote of a MAJORITY OF ALL THE MEMBERS OF THE BOARD (i.e., majority of the total number of directors, not merely of those present), so a majority of 10 directors is 6 votes, regardless of the number actually present at the meeting.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Corporate officers are elected by the vote of a majority of the entire board of directors, not merely a majority of those present at the meeting.

prompt: The meeting of the Board of Directors is conducted
rationale: Under Sec. 52 of the RCC, unless the by-laws provide otherwise, regular meetings of the board of directors shall be held monthly.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Absent a contrary by-law provision, regular board of directors' meetings are held monthly under the RCC.

prompt: The appraisal right can be exercised for any reason. This applies to shareholders of: I. An Ordinary Stock Corporation; II. A Close Corporation
rationale: In an ordinary stock corporation, appraisal rights may be exercised only in specific instances enumerated by the RCC (e.g., amendment of AOI restricting rights, sale of substantially all assets, merger/consolidation, investment in another business, extension/shortening of corporate term). In a CLOSE corporation, however, Sec. 104 of the RCC grants a stockholder the right to compel the corporation to purchase his shares 'for any reason,' provided the corporation has sufficient assets to cover its debts and liabilities exclusive of capital stock.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Only stockholders of a close corporation may exercise appraisal rights for any reason; in an ordinary stock corporation, appraisal rights are limited to specific statutory instances.

prompt: If a corporation opted to have a fixed term but wishes to extend the same, the extension shall be filed not earlier than __ years prior to the said expiration date:
rationale: Under Sec. 11 of the RCC, a corporation with a fixed corporate term may extend it by amending its Articles of Incorporation, and such amendment for extension must be filed with the SEC not earlier than three (3) years prior to the original or subsequent expiry date, unless the SEC allows an earlier filing justified by compelling reasons.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: An extension of a corporation's fixed term must generally be filed with the SEC not earlier than 3 years before the expiration date.

prompt: Under the Revised Corporation Code, continuous inoperation for a period of _____ would result in _____
rationale: Under Sec. 21 of the RCC, if a corporation has been continuously inoperative for at least five (5) years, the SEC may place it under delinquent status, which is a ground for suspension or revocation, rather than an automatic dissolution.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Continuous inoperation of a corporation for at least five years places it under delinquent status with the SEC, a precursor to possible revocation, not automatic dissolution.

prompt: Elbaf Corporation has its principal office in Elbaph Building, Tanza, Cavite. The building is too small to house its stockholders. Which of the following can be a valid venue for the stockholders meeting?
rationale: Under Sec. 50 of the RCC, stockholders'/members' meetings of corporations with principal offices outside Metro Manila may be held in the city or municipality where the principal office is located, i.e., the meeting must be held within Tanza, Cavite (the city/municipality of the principal office), not merely anywhere within the province or region.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A stockholders' meeting must be held in the city or municipality where the corporation's principal office is located, as stated in the Articles of Incorporation.

prompt: The directors of an ordinary stock corporation generally have a term of:
rationale: Under Sec. 22 of the RCC, directors of an ordinary stock corporation are elected for a term of one (1) year and shall hold office until their successors are elected and qualified.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Directors of an ordinary stock corporation serve a one-year term, holding over until successors are elected and qualified.

prompt: Which corporate officer is required to be a resident and a citizen of the Philippines?
rationale: Under Sec. 24 of the RCC, the corporate secretary must be a resident and citizen of the Philippines; the treasurer must be a resident (but need not be a Filipino citizen unless required by a special law); the president must be a director but there is no citizenship/residency requirement under the RCC itself.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Revised Corporation Code requires the corporate secretary (unlike the president or treasurer) to be both a Filipino citizen and a Philippine resident.

prompt: Where there are no creditors affected, the voluntary dissolution of a corporation would require a vote of ___ from the stockholders:
rationale: Under Sec. 134 of the RCC, voluntary dissolution where no creditors are affected requires a resolution adopted by the affirmative vote of the majority of the board of directors/trustees and a resolution duly approved by the affirmative vote of the stockholders owning at least a MAJORITY of the outstanding capital stock (or majority of members), not 2/3, 3/4, or unanimous.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Voluntary dissolution not affecting creditors requires only a majority vote of the outstanding capital stock (or members), together with board approval.

prompt: Gan Fall is a stockholder of Skypiea Corporation and owns 20% of its outstanding shares. Eneru owns 45%. How many shares would Gan Fall need to purchase from Eneru, at a minimum, to trigger the Mandatory Tender Offer Rule?
rationale: Under the SRC's Mandatory Tender Offer Rule, a tender offer is required when a person intends to acquire 35% or more of the equity of a public company in one or more transactions within a 12-month period, or when the acquisition would result in ownership of over 51%; it also applies to any acquisition that would result in ownership of over 50% when the acquirer already owns 20% or more. Here, Gan Fall already owns 20%; acquiring even just 31% more from Eneru (20% + 31% = 51%) would push his ownership beyond 50%, triggering the rule, whereas 30% only brings him to 50% exactly (not 'over' 50%).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Mandatory Tender Offer Rule is triggered when an acquisition brings the acquirer's total ownership to more than 50% of the outstanding shares of a public company (or 35% or more outright).

prompt: The resolutions adopted by the sole director of a One Person Corporation are recorded in a Minutes Book which would be a substitute for:
rationale: Under Sec. 128 of the RCC (One Person Corporations), since an OPC has only one stockholder who is also its sole director, there is no board meeting to hold; hence, the sole director's decisions are simply recorded in a Minutes Book, which serves as the substitute for minutes of the meeting that would otherwise be required for corporations with a multi-member board.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A One Person Corporation's Minutes Book, recording the sole director/stockholder's decisions, substitutes for the minutes of a board meeting since there is no multi-member board to convene.

prompt: A proxy may be allowed in: I. Stockholders' meeting; II. Directors' meeting
rationale: Proxy voting is expressly allowed for stockholders' or members' meetings under Sec. 57 of the RCC. Directors, however, being elected for their personal trust, confidence, and business judgment, cannot vote or attend board meetings by proxy; they must attend and act in person (or through remote communication, but not by proxy).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Proxy voting is allowed only in stockholders'/members' meetings; directors and trustees, occupying positions of trust, cannot vote by proxy in board meetings.

prompt: In case of a delinquency of a subscriber, which right is suspended and withheld until full payment of the subscription?
rationale: A delinquent stockholder loses the right to vote and be voted for, and to receive stock dividends, until the subscription is fully paid; however, unlike stock dividends, CASH dividends due on delinquent shares must still be applied to the unpaid balance of the subscription rather than being withheld outright as a suspended right — the classic tested distinction is that the right to receive STOCK dividends is withheld/suspended for delinquent shares.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Delinquent shares lose voting rights and are excluded from receiving stock dividends until the subscription is fully paid, although cash dividends thereon are instead applied to the unpaid balance.

prompt: The adoption of the by-laws after incorporation would necessitate _______ vote of the stockholders:
rationale: Under Sec. 45 of the RCC, when the by-laws are adopted AFTER incorporation (rather than filed simultaneously with the Articles of Incorporation), they must be approved by the affirmative vote of stockholders representing at least a majority of the outstanding capital stock (or members), and filed with the SEC.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: By-laws adopted after incorporation require approval by a majority of the outstanding capital stock or membership.

prompt: Thriller Bark Corporation has 5 directors, 2 vacancies occurred as follows: I. Gecko Moria retired; II. Ghost Princess Perona abandoned her seat. Which of the above vacancies would be filled up by the remaining directors?
rationale: Under Sec. 28 of the RCC, vacancies in the board other than by removal or expiration of term (e.g., retirement, resignation, abandonment of office, or other causes) may be filled by the vote of at least a majority of the remaining directors, if still constituting a quorum; both retirement and abandonment fall under this category, so both vacancies may be filled by the remaining directors (subject to ratification requirements as applicable).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Vacancies in the board arising from causes other than removal or expiration of term (such as retirement or abandonment) may be filled by a majority vote of the remaining directors constituting a quorum.

prompt: Alternative Certification of the Financial Statements would be allowed for corporation whose total assets or liabilities are less than P600,000. In which case, the certification will be done by:

choices.text: The president and a responsible officer
The treasurer and a responsible officer

rationale: Under SEC rules on financial statement requirements, corporations with total assets or liabilities of less than P600,000 may submit financial statements with an alternative (non-CPA-audited) certification, signed jointly by the corporation's president and treasurer, attesting to the correctness of the FS.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Small corporations below the P600,000 asset/liability threshold may submit financial statements certified jointly by the president and treasurer instead of a full independent audit.

prompt: Which of the following is false with regards to a close corporation?

choices.text: The number of stockholders cannot exceed 20
The stockholders may directly manage the corporation
The shares are prohibited from being listed in a stock exchange
The pre-emptive right can be denied in order to meet minimum public ownership

rationale: A close corporation's shares are, by definition, NOT listed in any stock exchange and are held by a limited number of persons (not more than 20), and stockholders may manage the business directly without a board (Sec. 96-97, RCC). Choice (d) is false because a close corporation, by its nature, does not have publicly-traded shares and thus has no 'minimum public ownership' requirement to meet; denial of pre-emptive rights in close corporations is allowed under different grounds (e.g., stated in the AOI), not for MPO compliance which applies to publicly-listed companies.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A close corporation is characterized by a cap of 20 stockholders, non-listing of shares in any stock exchange, and the option for direct stockholder management; it has no 'minimum public ownership' requirement since its shares are not publicly traded.

prompt: X Drake is a director in SWORD Corporation and BEAST PIRATES Corporation. The two corporations had a transaction with each other. What would be the ownership of X Drake in the corporations that would make the transaction voidable at the option of SWORD?
rationale: Under Sec. 32 of the RCC on contracts between corporations with interlocking directors, if the interest of the interlocking director in one of the corporations is merely 'nominal' (not exceeding 20% of the outstanding capital stock), the contract is valid subject only to the same disclosure/fairness safeguards for self-dealing directors; but if his interest exceeds 20% in either corporation, his interest is deemed 'substantial,' and the transaction is treated in the same manner as a contract between the corporation and its own director, i.e., voidable at the corporation's option absent the required ratification. Here, X Drake's 25% interest in BEAST PIRATES is substantial, making the contract voidable at SWORD's option.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Where an interlocking director's interest exceeds 20% (deemed 'substantial') in either contracting corporation, the contract is treated as a self-dealing director's contract and is voidable at the option of the corporation absent proper ratification.

prompt: A One Person Corporation's sole stockholder is also its sole director. Which corporate officer position is he/she not allowed to occupy?
rationale: Under Sec. 130 of the RCC, the single stockholder of an OPC shall be the sole director and president, and may also assume the role of Treasurer, but cannot be the Corporate Secretary; the OPC must appoint a different natural person as Corporate Secretary (although he/she may simultaneously act as Treasurer if a bond is posted and notice is given to the SEC).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: In a One Person Corporation, the single stockholder/sole director may act as President and Treasurer, but a different natural person must be appointed as Corporate Secretary.

prompt: After dissolution, a corporation continues to be a body corporate for purposes of liquidation and winding-up for a period of:
rationale: Under Sec. 139 of the RCC, a dissolved corporation continues as a body corporate for three (3) years from the effective date of dissolution for purposes of winding up its affairs, prosecuting/defending suits, and disposing of and conveying its property.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A dissolved corporation retains its corporate existence for three years solely for purposes of liquidation, winding up, and settling its affairs.

prompt: Refers to an order or orders for the purchase or sale of security with the knowledge that a simultaneous order or orders of substantially the same size, time and price for the sale or purchase of such security has, or will be entered by or for the same or different parties.
rationale: Under the SRC's provisions on market manipulation, a 'matched order' involves entering an order to buy or sell a security with knowledge that a matching order of substantially the same size, time and price has been or will be entered by or for the same or different parties, creating a false appearance of active trading.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A matched order is a manipulative device where offsetting buy and sell orders of substantially the same size, price, and time are pre-arranged to create a false impression of market activity.

prompt: Which of the following best describes an ultra vires act?

choices.text: It is contrary to morals and public policy
It is not within the powers of the corporation and is illegal
It is not within the powers of the corporation and may be illegal

rationale: An ultra vires act is one that is beyond or outside the powers conferred upon the corporation by its Articles of Incorporation, the RCC, and other applicable laws; it is not necessarily illegal per se (an ultra vires act may be entirely lawful in itself, just not among the corporation's authorized powers), so it 'may be' but is not always illegal.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: An ultra vires act is one outside the corporation's express, implied, or incidental powers; it is distinct from an illegal act, though it may sometimes also be illegal.

prompt: A cooperative organized for the primary purpose of providing medical, dental and other health services.
rationale: Under the Philippine Cooperative Code (RA 9520), a Health Services Cooperative is organized primarily to provide medical, dental, and other health services to its members and qualified non-members.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A Health Services Cooperative is a type of cooperative organized specifically to render medical, dental, and other health-related services.

prompt: The general assembly may by a _______ vote of all its members with voting rights, present and constituting a quorum, delegate some of its powers to a smaller body of the cooperative:
rationale: Under the Cooperative Code, the general assembly may delegate certain of its powers to a representative or smaller body only upon the affirmative vote of at least three-fourths (3/4) of the members with voting rights present and constituting a quorum.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A cooperative's general assembly may delegate some of its powers to a smaller representative body only by a three-fourths vote of the voting members present at a quorum.

prompt: The Reserve Fund is required to at least ___ after five years of operations of a cooperative:
rationale: Under the Cooperative Code's allocation of net surplus, a cooperative must set aside at least ten percent (10%) of its net surplus to the Reserve Fund, and this allocation rate is increased for cooperatives that have been in operation for less than five years (typically higher, e.g., 50%) but reduces to at least 10% once the cooperative has been operating for more than five years.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A cooperative's mandatory allocation to its Reserve Fund is reduced to a minimum of 10% of net surplus once it has been operating for more than five years.

prompt: Special meetings of either the Board of Directors or General Assembly of the Cooperative would necessitate a notice of at least ______ before the meeting:
rationale: Under the Cooperative Code's rules on meetings, a special meeting of the general assembly or the board of directors of a cooperative requires a written notice sent to members/directors at least one (1) week prior to the scheduled date, stating the time, place, and purpose of the meeting.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Special meetings of a cooperative's board or general assembly require at least one week's prior written notice specifying the meeting's purpose.

prompt: The members of this committee are elected directly by the General Assembly:
rationale: Under the Cooperative Code, the Election Committee is composed of members elected directly by the General Assembly, tasked with overseeing the conduct of elections of officers of the cooperative, unlike other committees which may be appointed by the board.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Election Committee of a cooperative is unique among its committees in being composed of members directly elected by the General Assembly rather than appointed by the board.

prompt: Which of the following modes of government procurement does not involve any bidding?
rationale: Under RA 9184 (as amended by RA 12009, the New Government Procurement Act) and its IRR, Negotiated Procurement is an alternative method of procurement resorted to WITHOUT public bidding under specific exceptional circumstances (e.g., emergency cases, two failed biddings, small value procurement), whereas limited source bidding, competitive dialogue, and unsolicited offer with bid matching still involve a bidding/competitive process among qualified or invited participants.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Negotiated procurement is a mode of government procurement resorted to without conducting competitive public bidding, allowed only under specified exceptional circumstances.

prompt: This criteria for bid selection considers cost only:
rationale: Under the government procurement rules, the Lowest Calculated Bid (and subsequently, after post-qualification, the Lowest Calculated Responsive Bid) evaluates bids based on price/cost alone, in contrast to methods like Most Advantageous Bid or Highest Rated Bid, which also weigh technical or quality factors.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Lowest Calculated Bid method of bid evaluation is based solely on price/cost, without weighing non-price technical or quality factors.

prompt: Which right of an unpaid seller will require insolvency of the buyer?
rationale: Under the law on Sales, the unpaid seller's right of stoppage in transitu (Art. 1530-1535) may be exercised only when the buyer is or becomes INSOLVENT, allowing the seller to resume possession of goods while in transit and stop delivery; the rights of lien and resale do not require the buyer's insolvency.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Stoppage in transitu is an unpaid seller's remedy exercisable only while goods are in transit and only when the buyer has become insolvent.

prompt: Kinemon exclusively owns a parcel of land which he sold to his wife O-Tsuru on April 25. He again sold the same land to Momonosuke, 17 years old on April 30. Momonosuke took possession of the land in good faith, while O-Tsuru registered the sale. Who will have a better right?
rationale: Under the rules on double sales (Art. 1544), for immovable property, ownership belongs to the buyer who first registers the sale in good faith; however, the first sale here — from Kinemon to his wife O-Tsuru — is VOID under Art. 1490 (spouses cannot sell property to each other except in specific exceptions), so O-Tsuru's registration produces no effect since she acquired nothing to register. Between Kinemon and Momonosuke, despite Momonosuke's minority, possession in good faith of the only valid sale prevails, making Momonosuke's right superior (the sale to a minor is merely voidable, not void, and remains valid until annulled).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A sale between spouses is void under Art. 1490 of the Civil Code, so a subsequent buyer in good faith under a valid (even if voidable, as when the buyer is a minor) sale prevails over the void first sale despite the first buyer's registration.

prompt: Iceburg, the mayor of Water 7 and head of Galley-La Company, approaches Kokoro, the experienced sea train conductor, and says: "I need a train component that can safely withstand Aqua Laguna because we'll be transporting important cargo." Kokoro recommends a specific part, assuring him it's reliable even in extreme sea conditions. Iceburg trusts her expertise and uses it. However, during Aqua Laguna, the component fails, putting the cargo at risk. Which implied warranty applies?
rationale: Under Art. 1562 of the Civil Code, when the buyer makes known to the seller the particular purpose for which the goods are required and relies on the seller's skill or judgment to select suitable goods, there arises an implied warranty of fitness for that particular purpose; here, Iceburg disclosed the specific purpose (withstanding Aqua Laguna) and relied on Kokoro's expertise to select the component.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: An implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arises when the buyer relies on the seller's skill or judgment after making known the specific purpose for which the goods are needed.

prompt: Which of the following is a formal contract?

choices.text: Both Real Estate and Chattel Mortgage

rationale: A chattel mortgage is a formal (solemn) contract because Philippine law (the Chattel Mortgage Law) requires that it be recorded in a public instrument and registered in the Chattel Mortgage Register to be VALID (not merely to bind third persons); a pledge and real estate mortgage, while requiring registration to bind third parties, do not require a public document for their validity between the parties.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A chattel mortgage is a formal contract requiring registration in a public instrument for validity, unlike a pledge or real estate mortgage where such formality is required only to bind third persons.

prompt: The debtor/owner of the thing given as security will be allowed to sell/dispose of the thing even during the pendency of the contract as long as the creditor consents.

choices.text: Both Real Estate and Chattel Mortgage

rationale: In a pledge, since possession of the thing is transferred to the pledgee/creditor, the pledgor is deprived of the ability to freely dispose of it while pledged and needs the pledgee's consent to sell it, unlike in mortgages (real estate or chattel) where the mortgagor retains possession and generally may sell or dispose of the mortgaged property (subject to the mortgage lien following the property) even without the mortgagee's consent.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: In a pledge, because possession passes to the creditor, the debtor-pledgor may only sell the pledged thing with the pledgee's consent, unlike in a mortgage where the debtor retains possession and disposal rights.

prompt: Absolute ownership of the object is a requirement in which of the following? I. Pledge; II. Real Estate Mortgage; III. Chattel Mortgage
rationale: Under Arts. 2085 and 2093 of the Civil Code, one of the common essential requisites of pledge, real estate mortgage, and chattel mortgage is that the pledgor/mortgagor be the absolute owner of the thing pledged or mortgaged.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Absolute ownership by the pledgor/mortgagor of the object given as security is a common essential requisite of pledge, real estate mortgage, and chattel mortgage.

prompt: A specific price advantage of a consumer product exists when in fact it does not. This will be considered as _____ under the Consumer Protection Act
rationale: Under RA 7394 (Consumer Act), representing that a consumer product has a sponsorship, approval, characteristic, ingredient, use, benefit, or quantity (such as a price advantage) which it does not actually have is classified as a deceptive sales act or practice.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Falsely representing a nonexistent price or other advantage of a consumer product constitutes a deceptive sales act or practice under the Consumer Act.

prompt: How many total repair attempts will be necessary before providing notice in writing to the manufacturer/dealer that the buyer/consumer intends to invoke the Lemon Law?
rationale: Under RA 10642 (Philippine Lemon Law), the vehicle must undergo at least four (4) separate repair attempts for the same nonconformity, and it must still exhibit the defect, before the consumer may send a notice to the manufacturer/distributor/dealer manifesting intent to avail of the Lemon Law rights, giving the latter a final repair attempt.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Philippine Lemon Law requires at least four unsuccessful repair attempts for the same defect before the consumer may give the manufacturer/dealer notice invoking Lemon Law protection.

prompt: The administrative liability for the first offense does not exceed P100M in:
rationale: Under the Philippine Competition Act (RA 10667), the maximum administrative fine for a first offense — whether for anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position, or prohibited mergers and acquisitions — is up to P100,000,000, with a higher cap for subsequent offenses.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Under the Philippine Competition Act, the administrative fine for a first offense across anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position, and prohibited mergers is capped at P100 million.

prompt: The PCC will generally have 30 days to review the merger agreement, but this may be extended upto ___ days if the PCC requests for additional information:
rationale: Under the PCA's merger review process, the Philippine Competition Commission has 30 days (Phase 1 review) to determine if a further review is needed, and this initial period can be extended up to an additional 60 days (i.e., a Phase 2 review period) if the PCC requests additional information from the merging parties.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The PCC's initial 30-day merger review period may be extended by up to 60 additional days if it requests further information from the parties.

prompt: The following are covered by the confidentiality of bank deposits, except:

choices.text: Demand deposit in a universal bank
Time deposit in a rural bank
Savings account in a commercial bank
Investment in bonds issued by a bank

rationale: The Bank Secrecy Law (RA 1405) and the Law on Secrecy of Foreign Currency Deposits cover deposits (demand, savings, and time/trust deposits) with banks; an investment in BONDS issued by a bank is a debt security/investment instrument, not a 'deposit,' and is therefore not covered by bank deposit secrecy laws.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Bank deposit secrecy covers demand, savings, and time deposits held with banks, but does not extend to bonds or other debt securities issued by a bank, which are investments rather than deposits.

prompt: The following requires a court order for the inspection or examination of bank accounts, except:

choices.text: Cases of bribery and dereliction of duty of a public official
Where the money deposited is the subject of litigation
When the Commissioner determines the net estate of a deceased depositor
Cases involving unexplained wealth of a public official

rationale: Under RA 1405 and related jurisprudence, examination of deposits for bribery/dereliction of duty cases (RA 3019), litigation involving the money deposited, and unexplained wealth cases (RA 1379) require a prior court order; however, the BIR Commissioner may inquire into a decedent's bank deposits to determine the gross estate for estate tax purposes WITHOUT need of a court order, under the Tax Code (as amended by the TRAIN Law).

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The BIR Commissioner may examine a deceased depositor's bank accounts to determine the gross estate for estate tax purposes without a court order, unlike other statutory exceptions to bank secrecy that require one.

prompt: The maximum possible civil penalty for violation of the Truth in Lending Act is:
rationale: Under RA 3765 (Truth in Lending Act), a creditor who fails to comply with the disclosure requirements is civilly liable to the debtor for an amount equal to twice the finance charge required to be disclosed, with a minimum of P100 and a maximum of P10,000, or in an amount equal to actual damages, whichever is greater.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Truth in Lending Act imposes a civil penalty on non-compliant creditors ranging from a minimum of P100 to a maximum of P10,000 (or actual damages, if greater).

prompt: Violation of the truth in lending act

choices.text: None of the choices is correct

rationale: A creditor's failure to comply with the Truth in Lending Act's disclosure requirements does NOT invalidate the underlying loan/credit transaction, does not extinguish or deem the loan fully paid, and does not make the finance charge itself illegal; it merely subjects the creditor to the prescribed civil penalty (and possible criminal liability) for non-disclosure.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Non-compliance with the Truth in Lending Act's disclosure requirements does not void the loan contract or the finance charge; it merely exposes the creditor to statutory civil (and criminal) penalties.

prompt: The following accounts bore the name of Emporio Ivankov in a closed bank: Ivankov for Sabo P100,000; Ivankov in trust for Dragon P100,000; Ivankov for account of Kuma P100,000; Ivankov and/or Revolutionary Army Corporation P100,000. How much can Ivankov recover from the PDIC?
rationale: Under the PDIC Law and its IRR, all deposit accounts held by the same person, in the same right and capacity, are combined and insured up to the maximum of P500,000 per depositor per bank. 'ITF' or 'for' accounts (Ivankov for Sabo, in trust for Dragon, for account of Kuma) are considered accounts held in a fiduciary/representative capacity — the actual beneficiary is entitled to the insurance, not Ivankov personally — while the joint 'and/or' account with a corporation is a separate insurable right. As Ivankov's own account in his individual capacity, only P100,000 (his personal/individual deposit) is directly recoverable by him; the other listed accounts belong to different insured rights/capacities (the beneficiaries or the joint account), not to Ivankov individually.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: PDIC deposit insurance combines all accounts held by the same depositor in the same right and capacity, but 'in trust for' or 'for account of' arrangements insure the actual beneficiary, not the nominal named depositor, up to the statutory maximum coverage.

prompt: If a depositor has P300,000 in the Manila branch of a closed bank due to insolvency; and P200,000 in the Tokyo branch. How much is he entitled to claim from the PDIC?
rationale: PDIC deposit insurance covers deposits maintained in a depositor's own right in DIFFERENT BRANCHES of the SAME BANK within the Philippines, combined and insured up to the maximum coverage of P500,000; the Manila branch deposit of P300,000 is thus insured in full since it does not exceed the P500,000 cap. However, deposits in FOREIGN branches (e.g., Tokyo) of a Philippine bank are outside PDIC's insurance coverage, as PDIC insurance applies only to deposits maintained in the Philippines; hence only the P300,000 Manila deposit is claimable.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: PDIC deposit insurance covers deposits combined across a depositor's accounts in the same right within Philippine branches up to P500,000, but excludes deposits maintained in foreign branches of the bank.

prompt: The following predicate crimes are committed by public officials, except:
rationale: Under the AMLA (RA 9160, as amended), 'corruption of public officers' under the Revised Penal Code is actually a crime typically committed by a PRIVATE person who corrupts (bribes) a public officer, rather than a crime committed by the public official himself; malversation, graft and corrupt practices, and (direct/indirect) bribery are crimes committed by the public officer.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Among AMLA predicate crimes, malversation, graft and corrupt practices, and bribery are committed by the public officer, while corruption of public officers is committed by the private person who corrupts the official.

prompt: An auditing firm is considered a covered institution if it offers the following services, except:

choices.text: acting as a formation agent of juridical persons
acting as a director or corporate secretary of a company
managing of client money, securities or other assets

rationale: Under the AMLA as amended (RA 10927/RA 11521), 'covered persons' now include lawyers, accountants, and other professionals when they act as formation agents of juridical persons, act as (or arrange for another to act as) a director/corporate secretary/nominee shareholder, or manage client money, securities, or other assets — all three activities listed subject such professionals/firms to AMLA coverage, so none of the choices is an exception.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Professionals such as lawyers and accountants become AMLA-covered persons when they act as formation agents, corporate officers/nominees, or asset managers for clients.

prompt: For real estate transactions, a single cash transaction exceeding __________ will be considered a covered transaction:
rationale: Under AMLA regulations covering real estate developers/brokers as covered persons, a single cash transaction (or a series of related transactions within one banking day) involving real estate exceeding P7,500,000 or its equivalent is treated as a covered transaction subject to reporting requirements.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Real estate transactions exceeding P7,500,000 in cash are treated as covered transactions requiring AMLA reporting.

prompt: Suspicious transactions must be reported to the AMLC within ______ from occurrence:
rationale: Under the AMLA, covered persons must report suspicious transactions to the AMLC within one (1) working day from the time of determination that the transaction is suspicious, i.e., the next working day.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Suspicious transactions must be reported to the AMLC no later than the next working day from determination of their suspicious character.

prompt: Holding company systems are considered covered institutions under the AMLA because they are supervised and/or regulated by:
rationale: Under the AMLA as amended, holding companies that exercise control over an insurer are treated as covered persons because they are considered part of/supervised in relation to the insurance industry regulatory framework overseen by the Insurance Commission.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Holding companies that control insurance firms are AMLA-covered persons owing to their being subject to the Insurance Commission's regulatory oversight.

prompt: A court order is not necessary for the AMLC to investigate a bank account if the predicate crime involved is any of the following, except:
rationale: Under the AMLA, the AMLC may inquire into and examine bank deposits/investments WITHOUT a court order only in cases involving kidnapping for ransom, violations of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act, and hijacking, destructive arson, murder (including those perpetrated by terrorists), and terrorism/conspiracy to commit terrorism financing — ordinary homicide (not committed by terrorists or falling under the enumerated crimes) still requires a court order for the AMLC to examine bank accounts.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The AMLC may examine bank deposits without a court order only for specifically enumerated predicate crimes (e.g., kidnapping for ransom, drug offenses, terrorism-related crimes); ordinary homicide is not among these exceptions and still requires a court order.

prompt: Shaka finished a patentable invention in May of 2025. Lilith also finished the same invention separately in December of 2025. Shaka filed an application for a patent in December of 2026, while Lilith filed the application on May of 2026. Who is entitled to the patent assuming all requisites for the grant of a patent are applicable?
rationale: The Philippines follows the 'first-to-file' rule (Sec. 29, IP Code) rather than 'first-to-invent': as between two or more persons who made the same invention separately and independently of each other, the right to the patent belongs to the person who filed an application for such invention FIRST, regardless of who invented it first. Lilith filed in May 2026, ahead of Shaka's December 2026 filing, so Lilith is entitled to the patent despite Shaka having invented it earlier.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Under the first-to-file rule of the Intellectual Property Code, the patent is awarded to whoever files the application first, not to whoever invented it first.

prompt: The period of protection is 20 years from application:
rationale: Under the IP Code, a patent for an invention has a term of twenty (20) years from the filing date of the application; trademarks are protected for 10 years (renewable indefinitely), while copyright protection generally lasts for the life of the author plus 50 years (varying by type of work), not tied to a filing date.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A Philippine patent's term of protection is 20 years, counted from the filing date of the patent application.

prompt: Electronic documents and electronic data messages can be considered the functional equivalent of their written counterparts in the following requirements of the law, except:

choices.text: The law requires the contract to be in writing to be enforceable
The law requires the document be retained in its original form
The law requires the transaction be in writing to be valid

rationale: Under the Electronic Commerce Act (RA 8792) and its rules, electronic documents/data messages are given legal recognition as functional equivalents of paper documents for purposes of satisfying writing requirements (whether for validity, enforceability under the Statute of Frauds, or retention in original form) — the law recognizes their equivalence across all these situations, so none of the choices is an exception.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Electronic Commerce Act grants electronic documents and data messages legal recognition as functional equivalents of their written counterparts, whether the writing requirement pertains to validity, enforceability, or retention in original form.

prompt: If the originator or addressee of an electronic data message or electronic document has more than one place of business and there is an underlying transaction related thereto, the place of dispatch or receipt would be:

choices.text: The place with the closest relationship to the underlying transaction

rationale: Under the E-Commerce Act's rules on time and place of dispatch/receipt of electronic data messages, if a party has more than one place of business, the relevant place is the one that has the closest relationship to the underlying transaction; if there is no underlying transaction, the principal place of business governs; and if a party has no place of business, the habitual residence is used.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Where a party to an e-commerce transaction has multiple places of business, the place with the closest relationship to the underlying transaction governs the place of dispatch or receipt of an electronic data message.

prompt: The following are outside the scope of the Data Privacy Act, except:

choices.text: The classification, salary range and responsibilities of the Secretary of Finance
A permit granted to a telecommunications company
The name of a person as used in a historical book

rationale: Under Sec. 4 of the Data Privacy Act (RA 10173), information about public officers relating to their position/functions (including classification and salary range), information about grantees of government permits/licenses, and personal information necessarily processed for journalistic, artistic, literary, or research purposes (such as being named in a historical book) are all EXCLUDED from the coverage of the DPA; hence none of the choices is an exception — all are outside the DPA's scope.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Data Privacy Act excludes from its coverage information about public officers' functions/compensation, information tied to government-issued permits/licenses, and personal information incidentally processed for journalistic, literary, or historical purposes.

prompt: A person's face as captured in a photograph is considered a:
rationale: Under the Data Privacy Act, a photograph of a person's face, being information from which the identity of an individual is reasonably and directly ascertainable, constitutes 'personal information'; it does not automatically fall under 'sensitive personal information' (which covers specific categories like race, health, sexual life, criminal history, etc.) unless it reveals such sensitive attributes.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A photograph capturing a person's face is classified as personal information under the Data Privacy Act because it can be used to reasonably identify that individual.

prompt: The data subject shall be notified and given an opportunity to withhold consent to the processing in case of changes or any amendment to the information supplied or declared to the data subject. This describes which right of a data subject?
rationale: Under Sec. 16 of the Data Privacy Act, a data subject has the right to be notified and given the opportunity to withhold consent to the processing in case of changes to the information supplied or declared — this is a distinct facet, the right to withhold consent, from the more general right to be informed (informed consent), which pertains to the initial disclosure at the time information is first collected.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A data subject's right to withhold consent allows them to refuse further processing when there are changes or amendments to the previously supplied or declared personal information.

prompt: The maximum number of signatories allowed under the Ease of Doing Business Act is:
rationale: Under RA 11032 (Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act), the number of signatories for any application or request submitted to a government agency shall be limited to a maximum of three (3) signatures, to streamline processing and reduce red tape.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Ease of Doing Business Act caps the required number of signatories for any government application or request at a maximum of three.

prompt: The following constitutes a violation of the Ease of Doing Business Act, except:

choices.text: Imposition of additional requirements other than those listed in the Citizen's Charter
Failure to render government services within the prescribed processing time on any application or request without due cause
Failure to attend to applicants or requesting parties who are within the premises of the office or agency concerned prior to the end of official working hours and during lunch break

rationale: Under RA 11032, all of the enumerated acts constitute violations: imposing additional requirements beyond the Citizen's Charter, failing to act on applications within the prescribed processing time without due cause, and refusing to attend to applicants present within office premises before the end of official hours (including during lunch break, as 'no noon break' policy is mandated) are all expressly penalized violations, so none is an exception.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The Ease of Doing Business Act penalizes imposing extra requirements beyond the Citizen's Charter, failing to act within the prescribed processing time, and refusing to serve applicants present before the close of official hours, including during lunch break.

prompt: In which of the following proceedings of the FRIA can there be a standstill period not exceeding 120 days agreed upon by the debtor and his creditors?
rationale: Under the FRIA (RA 10142), an out-of-court or informal restructuring/rehabilitation agreement (OCRA) may include a standstill period, not exceeding 120 days, during which the debtor and participating creditors agree to suspend actions/claims to allow negotiation of a restructuring/rehabilitation plan.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: An out-of-court rehabilitation agreement under the FRIA may include a negotiated standstill period of up to 120 days during which creditors refrain from enforcing claims.

prompt: The cram down effect applies to all of the following types of rehabilitation, except:
rationale: Under the FRIA, the 'cram down' effect — whereby an approved rehabilitation plan binds the debtor and all creditors, including dissenting ones and those who did not participate, upon court confirmation — applies to court-supervised rehabilitation, pre-negotiated rehabilitation, and even out-of-court/informal restructuring agreements once approved/confirmed as provided by law; hence none is an exception.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: The FRIA's cram-down effect, which binds all creditors (including dissenters) to an approved rehabilitation plan, applies across court-supervised, pre-negotiated, and out-of-court rehabilitation proceedings.

prompt: Involuntary rehabilitation of a juridical person would require creditors whose claim or aggregate claims is the higher between 25% of the subscribed capital or partners' contribution or at least
rationale: Under Sec. 12 of the FRIA, a petition for involuntary rehabilitation of a juridical debtor may be filed by any creditor or group of creditors with a claim of, or claims aggregating, at least Php1,000,000 or at least twenty-five percent (25%) of the subscribed capital stock or partners' contributions, whichever is higher.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A petition for involuntary rehabilitation requires creditor claims of at least P1,000,000 or 25% of the debtor's subscribed capital/partners' contributions, whichever is higher.

prompt: If a petition for rehabilitation is filed, but the court finds that there is no substantial likelihood of rehabilitation, the course of action would be:

choices.text: To give due course to the petition
To convert the proceeding into one of liquidation

rationale: Under the FRIA, if the court, after initially giving due course to the rehabilitation petition, later determines that there is no substantial likelihood that the debtor can be rehabilitated, it shall convert (motu proprio or upon motion) the proceedings into one for the liquidation of the debtor.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A rehabilitation proceeding is converted into liquidation once the court determines there is no substantial likelihood that the debtor can be successfully rehabilitated.

prompt: The court has 120 days to approve a pre-negotiated rehabilitation plan, otherwise:
rationale: Under Sec. 76 of the FRIA on pre-negotiated rehabilitation, if the court fails to act on the petition (approve or disapprove the pre-negotiated plan) within 120 days from the filing thereof, the rehabilitation plan is deemed approved by operation of law.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A pre-negotiated rehabilitation plan under the FRIA is deemed approved by operation of law if the court fails to act on it within 120 days.

prompt: A bounced check given as payment for a pre-existing obligation may be the source of liability under:
rationale: Estafa under Art. 315(2)(d) of the Revised Penal Code requires that the check be issued as the efficient cause/inducement for the offended party to part with money or property (i.e., simultaneous with or prior to the delivery of the consideration); a check issued merely in payment of a PRE-EXISTING obligation does not give rise to estafa since deceit is not the efficient cause of the transaction, but it may still give rise to liability under BP 22 (Bouncing Checks Law), which penalizes the mere act of issuing a worthless check regardless of the purpose for which it was issued.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: A check issued for a pre-existing obligation cannot give rise to estafa (since deceit did not induce the delivery of value), but it may still constitute a violation of BP 22, which punishes the issuance of a worthless check regardless of purpose.

prompt: In violations of BP Blg 22, the drawer must be notified of the bounced check and from such notice he is given _____ to make good the check or make arrangements for its payment.
rationale: Under BP 22, upon receiving notice of dishonor, the drawer is given five (5) banking days within which to make good the check (i.e., pay the amount or make arrangements for payment) to avoid the presumption of knowledge of insufficiency of funds and criminal liability.

source.center: ReSA - The Review School of Accountancy

canonicalConcept: Under BP 22, a drawer notified of a dishonored check has five banking days from receipt of notice to make the check good or arrange payment before the presumption of knowledge of insufficient funds attaches.
